messages.content:
Work out the ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Think in three steps: first name the condition chiefly responsible for the admission, second name the ICD-10-AM chapter letter it belongs to, third give the three-character category.

Example 1
Hospital course: A 72-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history was admitted with three days of worsening breathlessness and purulent sputum. Spirometry showed an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.52. He was treated with nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone and antibiotics for an infective exacerbation of his long-standing airflow limitation.
Answer: Irreversible airflow limitation in a heavy smoker with an infective exacerbation is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chapter J, category J44.
CODE: J44

Example 2
Hospital course: A 58-year-old man presented with crushing central chest pain radiating to the jaw. The electrocardiogram showed ST elevation in the anterior leads and high-sensitivity troponin rose from 40 to 2100 ng/L. He underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention with a stent to the proximal left anterior descending artery.
Answer: ST elevation with a rising troponin and culprit-vessel stenting is an acute myocardial infarction, chapter I, category I21.
CODE: I21

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Gender: Male
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]
Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Hospital Course:
The patient presented to the emergency department with right-sided chest pain and dyspnoea. Chest radiograph revealed a large right-sided pneumothorax. A pigtail intercostal catheter was inserted and placed on suction. The patient used nocturnal NIV and mouthpiece intermittent positive pressure ventilation (MIPPV) throughout the admission. The ICC was removed on day three, and the patient was discharged on day five with advice to cease all MI-E until clinical review in two weeks.

Follow-up:
At review, the MI-E pressures were decreased by a physiotherapist with instructions to use sparingly for cough augmentation or saliva clearance only. Pharmacological modalities of saliva management were recommended; however, the patient had no success with these previously. Unfortunately, the patient represented on three occasions with right-sided pneumothorax in the following six months, with chemical pleurodesis conducted twice, both of which failed to prevent recurrence. The patient was discharged home with a long-term pleural catheter after the fourth admission, which was removed two months later. The patient continues to use MI-E sparingly and has had no subsequent recurrence.

Instructions:
The patient is advised to continue using NIV and MIPPV. The patient should use MI-E sparingly for cough augmentation or saliva clearance only, as instructed by the physiotherapist. The patient should seek medical attention if he experiences any chest pain or dyspnoea. The patient should also pay attention to the signs of right-sided pneumothorax in the future and seek prompt medical attention if these occur again.

Write your reasoning in at most three short sentences, then a final line of exactly 'CODE: <letter><digit><digit>'.

text:
The condition chiefly responsible for the admission is a large right-sided pneumothorax, treated with an intercostal catheter. It was likely a secondary pneumothorax associated with mechanical insufflation-exsufflation (MI-E) in a ventilator-dependent patient. If it were documented as a procedural complication, J95 could apply instead, but as described it codes to pneumothorax, chapter J, category J93.

CODE: J93
